full_judgment: 16. Now, turning to the second contention it appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division had, in relying upon exhibits F & G, dakhila and a certified copy of khatian respectively, came to the conclusion that the appellants ceased to have any subsisting interest in the holding during the pendency of the preemption proceeding and could not, therefore, claim the right of pre-emption. In support of this conclusion the case of Chandra Kutner Maladas v. Abdul Matalbed, (1967) 19 DLR SC 36, was referred to. According to the Supreme Court of Pakistan, a co-sharer means a person whose interest subsists throughout the course of the application to pre-empt and not a person who held such interest in the beginning but lost it before its disposal. It was, therefore, held that a pre-emptor must not only have a subsisting interest in the holding when he files an application for pre-emption but must continue to hold the self-same interest till the date when the case is finally disposed of. Without disputing the proposition of law laid down in this case, the question that has to be resolved is whether the appellants ceased to be co-sharers if it is established that the jama in question was split up behind the back of the appellants. In other words, whether exhibits F & G produced a legal effect on the subsistence of the appellants interest so as to defeat their right to pre-empt the sale in question, if these exhibits are shown to have been obtained unilaterally without serving notice upon the appellants.
